chung.Syllabus Name: Blockchain and decentralized finance _Công nghệ Blockchain và Tài chính phi tập trung
chung.Time Allocation: Study hour (150h) = 45h (60 sessions) contact hours + 1h final exam + 104h self-study
chung.Description: This course introduces blockchain technology and its applications in cryptocurrencies and decentralized finance (DeFi). It covers cryptographic primitives (hash functions, digital signatures), blockchain data structures (blocks, Merkle trees), network architecture (nodes, mempool), consensus mechanisms and security (PoW/PoS, forks, double spending, 51% attack), and the evolution from Bitcoin to smart-contract platforms. The DeFi part focuses on financial primitives and protocols such as stablecoins, decentralized exchanges and automated market makers (AMMs), liquidity pools, tokenization and NFTs, governance via DAOs, and key issues in risk management, security, and regulation. Students will practice using wallets, block explorers, and smart-contract sandboxes; analyze real-world DeFi cases and on-chain data; and propose a DeFi/FinTech solution with clear assumptions, risks, and compliance considerations.
chung.StudentTasks: Students must attend at least 80% of contact sessions to be eligible for the final assessment. - Complete required readings and pre-class preparation; actively participate in discussions, case analyses, and in-class exercises. Complete and submit all quizzes/assignments/labs/projects on time; contribute fairly and professionally in group work. Follow academic integrity rules (no plagiarism, proper citation, no unauthorized collaboration); use AI tools responsibly and transparently when allowed by the instructor. - Use laptops/tablets in class strictly for learning activities. For hands-on blockchain labs: use testnets/sandbox accounts unless explicitly instructed; do NOT share private keys/seed phrases; follow security best practices.
chung.Note: Notes: - Blockchain & DeFi evolve rapidly; readings, examples, and tool versions may be updated during the semester. - The course is for educational purposes only and is NOT investment advice. - Students are not required to use real funds; labs can be completed fully on test networks.

clo: Explain blockchain fundamentals and describe how consensus mechanisms of PoW, PoS prevent double spending and maintain transaction integrity.
Describe the operating principles of Ethereum, smart contracts, gas fee economics, oracles and identify basic scaling approaches (Layer 1 sharding vs. Layer 2 rollups & payment channels).
Differentiate between stablecoin models and CBDCs, explaining their peg mechanisms and operational and liquidity risks.
Explain core DeFi market mechanisms, including Automated Market Makers, liquidity pools (impermanent loss), DAO governance models, and real-world asset tokenization.
Practice essential Web3 user operations, including setting up and securing non-custodial wallets, key management, executing testnet transactions, and participating in basic DAO voting.
Demonstrate basic DeFi user interactions on testnets and use public blockchain explorers/analytics dashboards to track transactions and protocol metrics.
danhGia: In-depth case analysis of a prominent real-world DeFi protocol (e.g., MakerDAO, Uniswap, Compound, Aave) or tokenization model; extracting on-chain metrics via DefiLlama/Etherscan, explaining protocol workflow, and identifying basic operational and liquidity risks.

cauHoiKienTao: Why isn’t blockchain “just an Excel database”? Identify which properties are essential for DeFi, and justify with one concrete DeFi use case.
In a trustless setting (no bank), how can a digital payment system prevent double spending?
A single transaction in a block is modified. Why does this matter for scalability and light verification?
Two miners produce two valid blocks at the same height. Explain how a P2P network resolves this fork. What does “finality” mean for DeFi trades and liquidations?
Miners/validators spend resources to secure the network. Using incentives, explain why honest behavior can be rational. Under what conditions could attacks become more feasible?
During congestion, how are transactions selected from the mempool (fees, size, waiting time, validity)?
What are the impacts on DeFi protocols (DEX swaps, lending, collateral liquidations)? Suggest practical risk mitigations.
A user signs the wrong transaction or approves a malicious smart contract. Why is it hard to reverse on-chain?
